title: No True Scotsman
objective: After this level you can spot the move that redefines a group to wave away a counterexample.
summary: Antony Flew's Scotsman rescues a generalization by redefining the group after a counterexample. The claim survives but becomes true by definition and says nothing.

cards.headline: "No Scot would do such a thing!" Then came the news from Aberdeen.
cards.body: In a story told by the philosopher Antony Flew, a Scotsman reads about a shocking crime in an English town and declares that no Scot would do such a thing. Soon he reads of something worse, done by a man in Aberdeen. His reply: "No true Scotsman would do such a thing!"

cards.headline: The move
cards.body: Flew named the fallacy after that story. It's a rescue: faced with a counterexample to a generalization, the speaker redefines the group so the counterexample no longer counts. The claim survives, but only because the rules changed after the evidence came in.

cards.headline: True, and empty
cards.body: "No real fan leaves early" sounds like news about fans, something you could test at any stadium. After the rescue, anyone who leaves early isn't a real fan, so the claim is true by definition. It gains truth and loses information: now it tells you only how the speaker uses the word "fan".

mascot.line: It connects: Level 4's factual claims can be checked. Once a claim is true by definition, there's nothing left to check.

cards.headline: Warning signs
cards.body: Watch for "true", "real" and "genuine" in front of an ordinary noun: true fans, real cooks, genuine gamers. A strict definition can be fair, but it should be set out before the counterexample shows up. A standard invented afterward is just moving the goalposts. So ask before you look: what would count against this claim?

cards.headline: No true Scotsman: exposed
learned: The move redefines a group to dodge a counterexample
Antony Flew named it after a story about a Scot
The claim becomes true by definition, and empty

questions.prompt: Which philosopher's story gave the "No true Scotsman" fallacy its name?

options.label: Bertrand Russell
options.rationale: Russell gave the firm, obstinate, pig-headed conjugation.

questions.explanation: Antony Flew named the move after his story of the Scotsman and the Aberdeen report.

questions.prompt: How does the "No true Scotsman" move protect a generalization?

options.label: It finds new evidence for the claim
It redefines the group to shut out the counterexample
It attacks the person who raised the counterexample
options.rationale: It changes a definition, not the subject.

options.label: It admits the generalization was wrong
options.rationale: The whole point is to avoid admitting that.

questions.explanation: The counterexample is ruled out by redefining the group after the fact.

questions.prompt: After the rescue, why can't observation check "No real fan leaves early" any more?

options.label: It has become true by definition
Fans' behavior can't be observed
options.rationale: You can watch who leaves; it just no longer counts.

options.label: It has turned into a question
It is now a matter of taste
options.rationale: It's a definition, not a taste.

questions.explanation: A factual claim can be checked by observation, but a claim true by definition can't be caught out by any fan.
